one_liner: C minimal-perfect-hash library (BDZ/CHD/BRZ) plus cxxmph::mph_map, claimed 10-50% faster than std::unordered_map on >100k URLs.
what_it_does: cmph builds a function that maps a fixed set of n unique keys to distinct ids in [0,n), or [0,m) for the non-minimal PHF variants. The C API builds from an I/O adapter (newline file, char* vector, struct array), queries with cmph_search(), and serializes with cmph_dump/cmph_load or packs into one contiguous blob with cmph_pack; values live in your own array indexed by the returned id. The experimental cxxmph layer (--enable-cxxmph) wraps BDZ in cxxmph::mph_map (aliases unordered_map, hash_map), dense_hash_map and sparse_hash_map templates that mimic the std::unordered_map / sparsehash interfaces for the common find/insert/erase/operator[]/iteration subset.
how_it_is_fast: The core is BDZ (Botelho, Pagh, Ziviani): each key hashes to one edge of a random 3-partite 3-uniform hypergraph; construction peels degree-1 vertices to prove the graph acyclic, then assigns 2-bit g values so that (g[v0]+g[v1]+g[v2]) mod 3 selects a slot unique to that key. In cxxmph a lookup is one MurmurHash3 x64_128 call, three 2-bit reads from a table of about 2.93 bits per bucket, a presence bit and at most one key comparison, with no chain walk or probe sequence; that is why the header says gains grow with key size, set size and miss rate. mph_map uses the non-minimal PHF (~81% slot occupancy, modulo), dense_hash_map rounds partitions to a power of two so a mask replaces the modulo (~50% occupancy), and sparse_hash_map adds a rank table for a minimal, 100%-occupied layout at extra lookup cost. The C library also offers CHD (~2.07 bits/key, fastest build) and BRZ (external-memory build for billions of keys).
when_to_use: Read-mostly string-keyed maps with 100k+ long keys (URLs, paths) that are expensive to compare, especially with many lookup misses: the header's only stated win case. Bulk-load, call rehash(), then serve lookups.
Assigning dense ids to a fixed set of 10^6 to 10^9 keys (URLs, words, n-grams) through the C API, with values stored in your own array indexed by the id.
Key sets that do not fit in RAM: the BRZ algorithm builds in external memory with a memory budget (-M) and temp dir, producing functions under 8 bits/key.
You need a compact, serializable static index: CHD ~2.07 bits/key or BDZ ~2.6 bits/key, dumped to a file or packed with cmph_pack into a blob that can be mmapped and queried with cmph_search_packed.
when_not_to_use: Insert-heavy or interleaved insert/lookup workloads: new keys go to a side std::unordered_map that every lookup checks first, and when the value vector fills the whole BDZ index is rebuilt in O(n).

Small maps, integer keys or cheap comparisons: the author warns the classes 'are not necessarily faster than their existing counterparts' and gives a figure only for >100k URLs; no numbers exist for other shapes.

Code that relies on std::unordered_map guarantees: any insert can relocate every element (invalidating all iterators and references), value_type is pair<Key, Data> so keys are mutable through iterators, the Alloc parameter is unused, and count/at/emplace/equal_range/reserve are missing.
Looking up keys that were not in the build set through the C API: cmph_search returns an arbitrary id for them (zvelo issue #4), so you must store and compare the keys yourself.

Projects that need a maintained or MSVC-ready codebase from this URL: the zvelo copy is frozen at 2012, cxxmph uses __builtin_expect and POSIX random(), and in this copy every mph_map unit test except erase_iterator is commented out.

integration.form: shared lib (autotools/libtool builds libcmph, and libcxxmph with --enable-cxxmph); cxxmph is 'header-mostly' and can be source-dropped as mph_map.h plus mph_index.cc, trigraph.cc, mph_bits.cc and MurmurHash3.cpp
integration.dependencies: none at runtime beyond libm; autotools to build; the check library only for the optional unit tests
integration.min_toolchain: C library: portable C with autotools. cxxmph: C++11 (configure adds -std=c++0x or gnu++0x) on GCC or Clang
integration.platforms: C library: GNU/Linux and WIN32, reported to work on OpenBSD and Solaris (README). cxxmph: GCC/Clang on POSIX systems, because of __builtin_expect and random(). No SIMD or architecture requirements.
integration.thread_safety: not documented; cxxmph's const find() does not modify state, so concurrent readers of a fully built map look safe, but any insert can rebuild the whole table and index construction calls the global random()
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — cxxmph::unordered_map/mph_map mirror find, insert, erase, operator[], begin/end, size, clear and rehash, but iterators are forward-only with no postfix ++, keys are not const, the allocator is ignored, several members are missing, and iterator/reference stability is much weaker than std::unordered_map

gotchas: In the zvelo copy, MPHIndex owns a raw new[] rank table and defines no copy constructor, so copying or assigning a populated map double-frees it; bonitao/cmph replaced it with std::vector.

A failed build is fatal: if BDZ finds no acyclic hypergraph in 1000 random seeds, mph_map::pack() calls exit(-1). Keys other than strings and built-in integers are hashed through std::hash truncated to 32 bits, so two keys that share those 32 bits collide for every seed and trigger this; by the birthday bound that is a real risk from about 10^5 keys.

Call rehash() after bulk loading (the benchmark does this before timing): until then pack() keeps twice the slot count reserved and recent inserts sit in the slack map. rehash() shrinks to fit, so the first insert after it triggers a full rebuild.

C API input must be duplicate-free, or the build fails with 'Unable to create minimum perfect hashing function' (FAQ, zvelo issue #2). An open report (bonitao issue #5) describes a memcpy pointer-arithmetic bug in BRZ's buffer_entry.c; the same line is present in this copy.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick cmph when the key set is built at run time and is far too large for compile-time tables such as frozen, constexpr-phf or ConstexprCore/perfect_hash: 10^6 to 10^9 keys, a serialized or mmapped function, or an external-memory build with BRZ. For a runtime std::unordered_map replacement, fph-table's dynamic perfect-hash map has published figures; cxxmph::mph_map has only an unquantified header claim.
verified_claims_summary: The only figure is the author's prose in mph_map.h: on large (>100k) URL sets the cxxmph maps were 'about 10%-50% faster than unordered_map'. The repo harness (bm_map.cc) runs 10M lookups over a 100k-URL file with StringPiece keys at 0% and 90% miss rates, plus 100k uint64 keys, against std::unordered_map with a Murmur3 hasher. The URL file is not shipped, no results are published, and neither compiler nor hardware is given; the header only advises -O3 -DNDEBUG.
status_note: zvelo/cmph is an abandoned 2012 import (last code change 2012-12-05; the 2017 commit only deleted a config file), so vendor the author's active repo github.com/bonitao/cmph instead: it has CI, recent commits (latest 2026-04-27, mostly tooling) and a fix for the rank-table copy bug, under the same LGPL-2.x / MPL-1.1 dual license.
